claim: Injured mature CNS axons do not regenerate in mammals.
source: Injured mature CNS axons do not regenerate in mammals.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Deletion of PTEN induces CNS axon regeneration through the activation of PI3K-mTOR signaling.
source: Deletion of PTEN, the negative regulator of PI3K, induces CNS axon regeneration through the activation of PI3K-mTOR signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Park et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2010) mentioned in the introduction.

claim: AKT3 induces much more robust axon regeneration than AKT1.
source: We found that the predominant AKT isoform in CNS, AKT3, induces much more robust axon regeneration than AKT1
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A,B comparing axon regeneration between AKT isoforms.

claim: Activation of mTORC1 is critical for AKT-induced axon regeneration.
source: activation of mTORC1 and inhibition of GSK3β are two critical parallel pathways for AKT-induced axon regeneration
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that Rptor deletion (which blocks mTORC1) significantly decreases AKT3-induced axon regeneration (Figure 6A,B).

claim: Inhibition of GSK3β is critical for AKT-induced axon regeneration.
source: activation of mTORC1 and inhibition of GSK3β are two critical parallel pathways for AKT-induced axon regeneration
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that GSK3β-S9A mutant significantly blocks AKT3-induced axon regeneration (Figure 7A,B).

claim: Phosphorylation of T308 and S473 of AKT play opposite roles in GSK3β phosphorylation and inhibition.
source: phosphorylation of T308 and S473 of AKT play opposite roles in GSK3β phosphorylation and inhibition
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that blocking S473 phosphorylation increases GSK3β-S9 phosphorylation (Figure 5B,H).

claim: mTORC2 and pAKT-S473 negatively regulate axon regeneration.
source: mTORC2 and pAKT-S473 negatively regulate axon regeneration
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that AKT3-S472A mutant and Rictor deletion enhance axon regeneration compared to WT AKT3 (Figure 4C,D).

claim: AAV2 has specific tropism for RGCs after intravitreal injection.
source: We and other investigators have demonstrated a specific tropism of AAV2 for RGCs after intravitreal injection (Park et al., 2008; Pang et al., 2008; Hu et al., 2012; Boye et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Capsid-mutated AAV2 (Y444, 500, 730F) achieves transduction exceeding 80% of RGCs.
source: transduction exceeded 80% of RGC, based on the ratio of HA (transgene tag) to Tuj1 (antibody for RGC marker, β-III tubulin) positive cells in flat-mount retinas (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: All three isoforms of AKT significantly increased levels of pAKT-S473 and pS6 in RGCs.
source: We also confirmed that all three isoforms of AKT produced the expected changes in RGCs: significantly increased levels of pAKT-S473 and pS6 (mTORC1 activation marker), indicating activation of AKT and mTORC1 (Figure 1A,B
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Levels of pT308 and pS6 were significantly higher in retinas transfected by AKT3 than by AKT1.
source: Western blot analysis of retina lysates showed comparable expression of AKT isoforms (HA levels), but levels of pT308 and pS6 were significantly higher in retinas transfected by AKT3 than by AKT1 (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: AKT2 and AKT3 caused significantly more axon regeneration than AKT1.
source: AKT2 and AKT3 caused significantly more axon regeneration than AKT1
evidence: This is supported by axon counting data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: AKT2 induced the longest axon growth among the three AKT isoforms.
source: AKT2 induced the longest axon growth (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by axon tracing data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: All three AKT isoforms increased RGC survival to more than 40%.
source: all three isoforms increased RGC survival to more than 40% based on Tuj1 staining in retinal flat-mounts, at least a 1-fold increase over WT mice
evidence: This is supported by RGC counting data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Significantly more RGCs survived in mice injected with AAV-AKT3 than with AKT1.
source: significantly more RGCs survived in mice injected with AAV-AKT3 than with AKT1 (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by RGC survival quantification shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: AKT3 is the predominant isoform in adult mouse brain, representing 50% of total AKT.
source: AKT3 is the predominant isoform in adult mouse brain (50% AKT3, 30% AKT1 and 20% AKT2) (Easton et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Easton et al., 2005.

claim: AKT1 and AKT3 are the two major isoforms of AKT in RGCs, each representing 45% of total AKT.
source: Measurement of transcript abundance in fragments per Kb of exon per million fragments mapped (FPKM) (Mortazavi et al., 2008) indicated that AKT1 and AKT3 were the two major isoforms of AKT in RGCs; each represented 45% of total AKT, a vivid contrast to AKT2 (10%) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E.

claim: AKT3 kinase dead (KD) mutant, T305A/S472A (AA) mutant, and single T305A mutant all showed significantly lower phosphorylation of T308, S473 and S6 than WT AKT3.
source: all three mutants showed significantly lower phosphorylation of T308, S473 and S6 than WT AKT3 (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and Western blot data shown in Figure 3.

claim: AKT3-KD, AA, and T305A mutants did not induce axon regeneration.
source: the three mutants did not induce axon regeneration (Figure 4A,B)
evidence: This is supported by axon tracing data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Phosphorylation of AKT-T308 and the kinase activity of AKT are critical for axon regeneration.
source: indicating that the phosphorylation of AKT-T308 and the kinase activity of AKT are critical for axon regeneration.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that kinase-dead and T308 mutants do not induce axon regeneration.

claim: AKT3-S472A mutant produced a small but statistically significant increase in axon regeneration at 500 µm distal to the crush site compared to WT AKT3.
source: the AKT3-S472A mutant produced a small but statistically significant increase in axon regeneration at 500 µm distal to the crush site and a trend toward increase at other distances, compared to WT AKT3 (Figure 4C,D)
evidence: This is supported by axon counting data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: pS473 inhibits the effect of AKT on axon regeneration.
source: suggesting that pS473 inhibits the effect of AKT on axon regeneration.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that blocking S473 phosphorylation enhances axon regeneration.

claim: mTORC2 is inhibitory for AKT-induced axon regeneration.
source: To confirm this unanticipated finding, we tested whether mTORC2 also is inhibitory for AKT-induced axon regeneration
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that Rictor deletion enhances AKT3-induced axon regeneration (Figure 4C,D).

claim: AKT3 and Rictor KO produced even more extensive and lengthier axon regeneration than AKT3 alone.
source: AKT3 and Rictor KO produced even more extensive and lengthier axon regeneration than AKT3 alone (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by axon tracing data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Rictor KO alone did not cause any axon regeneration.
source: This was not due to an additive effect because Rictor KO alone did not cause any axon regeneration (Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by axon tracing data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: AKT3-S472A mutant and Rictor deletion significantly decreased pS473 levels.
source: both immunostaining and Western blot analysis confirmed that AKT3-S472A mutant and Rictor deletion significantly decreased pS473 levels (Figure 5A,B,F).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and Western blot data shown in Figure 5A,B,F.

claim: Enhanced axon regeneration by AKT3-S472A and Rictor KO was not due to increased expression of AKT3.
source: The enhanced axon regeneration was not due to increased expression of AKT3, which was slightly decreased in Rictor KO mice (Figure 5B,D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5B,D.

claim: Enhanced axon regeneration by AKT3-S472A and Rictor KO was not due to enhanced activation of AKT or mTORC1.
source: It was also not due to enhanced activation of AKT or mTORC1, because levels of pT308 and pS6 were also decreased (Figure 5B,E,G).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5B,E,G.

claim: mTORC2 and pS473 have a negative effect on GSK3β-S9 phosphorylation.
source: mTORC2 and pS473 had a negative effect on GSK3β-S9 phosphorylation; deletion of Rictor significantly increased pGSK3β-S9 level (Figure 5B,H).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5B,H.

claim: Rictor KO alone did not increase pGSK3β-S9 compared to WT mice.
source: Rictor KO alone did not increase pGSK3β-S9 compared to WT mice (Figure 5C)
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: AKT kinase activity is required for GSK3β phosphorylation.
source: suggesting that AKT kinase activity is required for GSK3β phosphorylation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Rictor KO alone does not increase pGSK3β-S9.

claim: All three AKT isoforms and AKT3-S472A mutant were translocated into optic nerve.
source: All three AKT isoforms and AKT3-S472A mutant were translocated into ON.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The distribution in optic nerve of AKT3 mutants (KD, AA and T305A) that did not induce axon regeneration was significantly limited.
source: the distribution in ON of the three AKT3 mutants (KD, AA and T305A) that did not induce axon regeneration was significantly limited (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: AKT3 was present in regenerating axons.
source: AKT3 was also present in regenerating axons (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: AKT3 mutants (AKT3-KD, AA and T305A) significantly decreased survival of axotomized RGCs compared to WT AKT3.
source: the three AKT3 mutants (AKT3-KD, AA and T305A mutants) significantly decreased survival of axotomized RGCs compared to WT AKT3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by RGC survival data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Neither the AKT3-S472A mutant nor Rictor deletion significantly changed RGC survival.
source: Neither the AKT3-S472A mutant nor Rictor deletion significantly changed RGC survival (Figure 4—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This is supported by RGC survival data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Increased axon regeneration by AKT3-S472A and Rictor KO is not due to increased neuron survival.
source: indicating that increased axon regeneration is not due to increased neuron survival.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that RGC survival is unchanged despite enhanced axon regeneration.

claim: AKT kinase activity is required for both axon regeneration and RGC survival.
source: these results show that AKT kinase activity is required for both axon regeneration and RGC survival
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that kinase-dead mutants fail to promote both axon regeneration and RGC survival.

claim: Phosphorylation of T308 by PI3K-PDK1 and phosphorylation of S473 by mTORC2 play opposite roles in GSK3β phosphorylation/inhibition and axon regeneration.
source: phosphorylation of T308 by PI3K-PDK1 and phosphorylation of S473 by mTORC2 play opposite roles in GSK3β phosphorylation/inhibition and axon regeneration.
evidence: This is supported by multiple experimental observations showing differential effects of T308 and S473 phosphorylation on GSK3β and axon regeneration.

claim: Rptor deletion significantly decreased AKT3-induced axon regeneration.
source: Rptor deletion alone did not result in axon regeneration (Figure 4—figure supplement 1); it significantly decreased AKT3-induced axon regeneration (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is supported by axon tracing data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: S6K1-DN and 4E-BP1-4A significantly decreased AKT3-induced axon regeneration.
source: Similar to Rptor deletion, S6K1-DN and 4E-BP1-4A also significantly decreased AKT3-induced axon regeneration (Figure 6A,B)
evidence: This is supported by axon tracing data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: Deletion of Mtor significantly inhibited AKT3-induced axon regeneration.
source: Deletion of Mtor itself did not result in axon regeneration (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) but significantly inhibited AKT3-induced axon regeneration (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is supported by axon tracing data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: mTORC1 inhibition by deletion of Rptor or Mtor, or by overexpression of S6K1-DN and 4E-BP1-4A, significantly decreased AAV-AKT3 expression.
source: mTORC1 inhibition by deletion of Rptor or Mtor, or by overexpression of S6K1-DN and 4E-BP1-4A, significantly decreased the AAV-AKT3 expression (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: RGC survival was not changed by Rptor/Mtor KO or S6K1-DN and 4E-BP1-4A overexpression.
source: However, RGC survival was not changed by these manipulations (Figure 6E,F)
evidence: This is supported by RGC survival data shown in Figure 6E,F.

claim: GSK3β-S9A significantly blocked AKT3-induced axon regeneration.
source: GSK3β-S9A significantly blocked AKT3-induced axon regeneration (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is supported by axon tracing data shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: Combining Rptor deletion with GSK3β-S9A overexpression almost totally prevented AKT3-induced axon regeneration.
source: Combining Rptor deletion with GSK3β-S9A overexpression blocked both mTORC1 activation and GSK3β inhibition, which almost totally prevented AKT3-induced axon regeneration (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is supported by axon tracing data shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: Phosphorylation and inhibition of GSK3β and activation of mTORC1 are two parallel signal pathways downstream of AKT3 that act together to influence axon regeneration.
source: These results suggest that phosphorylation and inhibition of GSK3β and activation of mTORC1 are two parallel signal pathways downstream of AKT3 that act together to influence axon regeneration.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that blocking both pathways has an additive inhibitory effect on axon regeneration.

claim: Gsk3b KO alone induced a small but significant amount of axon regeneration.
source: Gsk3b KO alone induced a small but significant amount of axon regeneration, in dramatic contrast to the deletion of Gsk3a, which yielded no axon regeneration.
evidence: This is supported by axon tracing data shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: Deletion of Gsk3a yielded no axon regeneration.
source: in dramatic contrast to the deletion of Gsk3a, which yielded no axon regeneration.
evidence: This is supported by axon tracing data shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: Deletion of both Gsk3a and Gsk3b did not have an additive effect on axon regeneration.
source: Deletion of both Gsk3a and Gsk3b did not have an additive effect on axon regeneration (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by axon tracing data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: S6K1-CA expression in Gsk3b KO mice enhanced axon regeneration.
source: This experiment showed enhancement of axon regeneration when S6K1 constitutively active mutant (S6K1-CA) was expressed in Gsk3b KO mice (Figure 7C,D)
evidence: This is supported by axon tracing data shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: mTORC1 and GSK3β act in parallel, synergistic pathways downstream of AKT for axon regeneration.
source: consistent with the idea that mTORC1 and GSK3β act in parallel, synergistic pathways downstream of AKT for axon regeneration.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that activating mTORC1 and deleting Gsk3b have an additive effect on axon regeneration.

claim: Regenerating axons were more numerous and longer in Gsk3b KO mice injected with AAV-AKT3.
source: regenerating axons were more numerous and longer in Gsk3b KO mice injected with AAV-AKT3 (Figure 7E,F)
evidence: This is supported by axon tracing data shown in Figure 7E,F.

claim: RGC survival induced by AKT3 was unchanged after Gsk3b and/or Rptor manipulation.
source: RGC survival induced by AKT3 was unchanged (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C,D)
evidence: This is supported by RGC survival data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Deletion of AKT1 reduces whole body size.
source: Deletion of AKT1 reduces whole body size and deletion of AKT2 results in diabetes-like syndrome (Cho et al., 2001a; Cho et al., 2001b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cho et al., 2001a; Cho et al., 2001b.

claim: Deletion of AKT2 results in diabetes-like syndrome.
source: Deletion of AKT1 reduces whole body size and deletion of AKT2 results in diabetes-like syndrome (Cho et al., 2001a; Cho et al., 2001b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cho et al., 2001a; Cho et al., 2001b.

claim: Deletion of AKT3 specifically reduces brain size.
source: Deletion only of AKT3 specifically reduces brain size (Easton et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Easton et al., 2005.

claim: AKT2 and AKT3, but not AKT1, regulate survival and growth of cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: AKT2 and AKT3, but not AKT1, regulate survival and growth of cultured hippocampal neurons (Diez et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Diez et al., 2012.

claim: AKT3 KO, but not AKT1 deletion, decreases pS6 significantly in brain.
source: This is also true in brain as AKT3 KO, but not AKT1 deletion, decreases pS6 significantly (Easton et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Easton et al., 2005.

claim: 4E-BP inhibition and S6K activation promote protein synthesis.
source: Both 4E-BP inhibition and S6K activation promote protein synthesis
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of mTORC1 signaling.

claim: 4E-BPs act specifically to control cell proliferation (cell number).
source: but 4E-BPs act specifically to control cell proliferation (cell number) and S6Ks preferentially regulate cell growth (cell size) (Dowling et al., 2010; Ohanna et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dowling et al., 2010; Ohanna et al., 2005.

claim: S6Ks preferentially regulate cell growth (cell size).
source: but 4E-BPs act specifically to control cell proliferation (cell number) and S6Ks preferentially regulate cell growth (cell size) (Dowling et al., 2010; Ohanna et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dowling et al., 2010; Ohanna et al., 2005.

claim: S6K1 activation, but not 4E-BP inhibition, is sufficient for axon regeneration.
source: We previously reported that, although S6K1 activation, but not 4E-BP inhibition, is sufficient for axon regeneration, 4E-BP inhibition is necessary for PTEN deletion-induced axon regeneration (Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2014.

claim: 4E-BP inhibition is necessary for PTEN deletion-induced axon regeneration.
source: We previously reported that, although S6K1 activation, but not 4E-BP inhibition, is sufficient for axon regeneration, 4E-BP inhibition is necessary for PTEN deletion-induced axon regeneration (Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2014.

claim: Phosphorylation and inhibition of GSK-3β is critical for neuronal polarization, axon branching and axon growth.
source: Phosphorylation and inhibition of another AKT substrate, glycogen synthase kinase 3β (GSK-3β), is critical for neuronal polarization, axon branching and axon growth (Kim et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kim et al., 2011b.

claim: PI3K activates mTOR complex 2 (mTORC2) in a ribosome-dependent manner.
source: Although the mechanism is unclear, PI3K also activates mTOR complex 2 (mTORC2) in a ribosome-dependent manner (Zinzalla et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zinzalla et al., 2011.

claim: mTORC2 phosphorylates AKT at S473.
source: which in turn phosphorylates AKT at S473 (pS473) (Sarbassov et al., 2005; Guertin et al., 2006; Hresko and Mueckler, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sarbassov et al., 2005; Guertin et al., 2006; Hresko and Mueckler, 2005.

claim: pS473 enhances phosphorylation of AKT-T308.
source: pS473 enhances phosphorylation of AKT-T308 (Yang et al., 2002; Scheid et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yang et al., 2002; Scheid et al., 2002.

claim: Inhibition of S473 phosphorylation by destroying mTORC2 decreases AKT-T308 phosphorylation.
source: and inhibition of S473 phosphorylation by destroying mTORC2 decreases AKT-T308 phosphorylation (Sarbassov et al., 2005; Carson et al., 2013; Yuan et al., 2012; Hresko and Mueckler, 2005; Guertin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sarbassov et al., 2005; Carson et al., 2013; Yuan et al., 2012; Hresko and Mueckler, 2005; Guertin et al., 2009.

claim: mTORC2 is involved in cell survival and actin cytoskeleton dynamics.
source: mTORC2 is involved in cell survival and actin cytoskeleton dynamics (Jacinto et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jacinto et al., 2004.

claim: mTORC2 plays a role in lipogenesis and adipogenesis.
source: and, like mTORC1, plays a role in lipogenesis and adipogenesis (Yao et al., 2013; Lamming and Sabatini, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yao et al., 2013; Lamming and Sabatini, 2013.

claim: Liver or muscle-specific Rictor deletion increases GSK3β phosphorylation.
source: the liver or muscle-specific Rictor deletion increases GSK3β phosphorylation (Kumar et al., 2008; Yuan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kumar et al., 2008; Yuan et al., 2012.

claim: mTORC2 and pAKT-S473 are necessary for PTEN deletion-induced tissue overgrowth in drosophila eyes.
source: Since mTORC2 and pAKT-S473 are necessary for PTEN deletion-induced tissue overgrowth in drosophila eyes (Hietakangas and Cohen, 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hietakangas and Cohen, 2007.

claim: mTORC2 and pAKT-S473 are necessary for development of prostate cancer in mouse.
source: and development of prostate cancer in mouse (Guertin et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Guertin et al., 2009.

claim: Most corticospinal neurons exhibit long term survival after transection in the spinal cord.
source: For example, most corticospinal neurons exhibit long term survival after transection in the spinal cord (Nielson et al., 2010; 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nielson et al., 2010; 2011.

claim: Corticospinal neurons fail to regenerate axons after spinal cord transection.
source: but they fail to regenerate axons (Schwab and Bartholdi, 1996; Goldberg et al., 2002b; Fitch and Silver, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schwab and Bartholdi, 1996; Goldberg et al., 2002b; Fitch and Silver, 2008.

claim: 20% of RGCs normally survive ON crush in mice.
source: The 20% of RGCs that normally survive ON crush in mice can be increased significantly by inhibition of apoptosis, deleting tumor suppressor genes or by manipulating ER stress pathways
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of RGC survival after optic nerve injury.

claim: Inhibition of apoptosis, deleting tumor suppressor genes or manipulating ER stress pathways can increase RGC survival but do not necessarily induce ON regeneration.
source: The 20% of RGCs that normally survive ON crush in mice can be increased significantly by inhibition of apoptosis, deleting tumor suppressor genes or by manipulating ER stress pathways, but these manipulations do not necessarily induce ON regeneration (Park et al., 2008; Hu et al., 2012; Goldberg et al., 2002a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Park et al., 2008; Hu et al., 2012; Goldberg et al., 2002a.

claim: Axon regeneration requires neuronal intrinsic growth stimulators that are distinct from neuronal surviving factors.
source: This observation indicates that axon regeneration requires neuronal intrinsic growth stimulators that are distinct from neuronal surviving factors.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that increased survival does not necessarily lead to increased axon regeneration.

claim: There are far fewer regenerating axons than surviving RGCs.
source: There are far fewer regenerating axons than surviving RGCs, however, suggesting that only a small percentage of RGCs are regenerating
evidence: This is a general observation from the experimental data.

claim: Different subtypes of RGCs have different regeneration abilities.
source: and different subtypes of RGCs have different regeneration abilities (Duan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Duan et al., 2015.

claim: Localized protein synthesis is important for peripheral axon regeneration.
source: Increasing evidence has demonstrated the importance of localized protein synthesis in peripheral axon regeneration (Willis and Twiss, 2006; Jung et al., 2012; Perry and Fainzilber, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Willis and Twiss, 2006; Jung et al., 2012; Perry and Fainzilber, 2014.

claim: Intra-axonal translation has been demonstrated in mature mouse hippocampus.
source: Intra-axonal translation has recently been demonstrated in mature mouse hippocampus (Baleriola et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Baleriola et al., 2014.

claim: Certain mRNA species and components of translation machinery, including pS6 and 4E-BP1, have been detected in regenerating axons in rat spinal cord.
source: and, more intriguingly, certain mRNA species and additional components of translation machinery, including pS6 and 4E-BP1, have been detected in regenerating axons in rat spinal cord (Kalinski et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kalinski et al., 2015.

claim: Activation of mTORC1 and inhibition of GSK3β are two critical pathways downstream of AKT that act in parallel and synergistically to promote CNS axon regeneration.
source: our genetic manipulations in RGCs have established that the activation of mTORC1 and inhibition of GSK3β are two critical pathways downstream of AKT that act in parallel and synergistically to promote CNS axon regeneration (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by multiple experimental observations throughout the study.

claim: A balancing mechanism exists downstream of PI3K where AKT integrates both positive and negative signals through phosphorylation of T308 and S473.
source: The opposite effects of mTORC1 and mTORC2 on axon regeneration suggest that a balancing mechanism exists downstream of the critical growth-promoting signal PI3K and that AKT integrates both positive and negative signals through phosphorylation of T308 and S473 and their specific roles in downstream effectors mTORC1 and GSK3β to control CNS axon regeneration (Figure 8).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mTORC1 promotes while mTORC2 inhibits axon regeneration.

claim: mTORC1/S6K functions as feedback inhibition of PI3K signaling.
source: Interestingly, mTORC1/S6K also functions as feedback inhibition of PI3K signaling (Laplante and Sabatini, 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Laplante and Sabatini, 2012.

claim: PI3K is a lipid kinase that can be activated by receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK).
source: PI3K is a lipid kinase, which can be activated by receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) and subsequently phosphorylates phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) in the lipid membrane to produce phosphatidylinositol (3,4,5)-triphosphate (PIP3).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of PI3K signaling.

claim: PI3K phosphorylates PIP2 to produce PIP3.
source: PI3K is a lipid kinase, which can be activated by receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) and subsequently phosphorylates phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) in the lipid membrane to produce phosphatidylinositol (3,4,5)-triphosphate (PIP3).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of PI3K signaling.

claim: PIP3 recruits AKT to the membrane to be activated by phosphorylation at T308 via PDK1.
source: PIP3 in turn recruits AKT, a member of the AGC family of serine/threonine kinases, to the membrane to be activated by phosphorylation at T308 via phosphoinositide-dependent kinase-1 (PDK1) (Manning and Cantley, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Manning and Cantley, 2007.

claim: PTEN is a lipid phosphatase that converts PIP3 to PIP2.
source: PTEN is a lipid phosphatase that converts PIP3 to PIP2, and thus inhibits the activation of downstream effectors of PI3K.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of PI3K signaling.

claim: The PI3K-AKT pathway is the main effector by which RTKs promote cell survival and growth in response to growth factor signaling.
source: The PI3K-AKT pathway is the main effector by which RTKs promote cell survival and growth in response to growth factor signaling (Song et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Song et al., 2012a.

claim: AKT activation removes the inhibition of TSC and activates mTORC1.
source: Thus AKT activation removes the inhibition of TSC and activates mTORC1.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of mTOR signaling.

claim: The PI3K-AKT-mTORC1 pathway is a master regulator of protein synthesis and cellular growth.
source: The PI3K-AKT-mTORC1 pathway is a master regulator of protein synthesis and cellular growth (Manning and Cantley, 2007; Laplante and Sabatini, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Manning and Cantley, 2007; Laplante and Sabatini, 2012.

claim: Phosphorylation of 4E-BPs releases inhibition of eIF4E and initiates cap-dependent translation.
source: One of these is the eukaryotic initiation factor 4E-binding proteins (4E-BPs); their phosphorylation releases inhibition of eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E and initiates cap-dependent translation.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of mTORC1 signaling.

claim: Phosphorylation of S6Ks is critical for mRNA biogenesis, translation initiation and elongation.
source: The other is the ribosomal protein S6 kinases (S6Ks); their phosphorylation is critical for mRNA biogenesis, translation initiation and elongation (Hay and Sonenberg, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hay and Sonenberg, 2004.

claim: Phosphorylation of ribosome protein S6 (pS6) by S6K has often served as a marker for mTORC1 activation.
source: Phosphorylation of ribosome protein S6 (pS6) by S6K has often served as a marker for mTORC1 activation.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of mTORC1 signaling.

claim: S6K functions as feedback inhibition of RTK/PI3K signaling.
source: Interestingly, S6K also functions as feedback inhibition of RTK/PI3K signaling, which balances mTORC1 activation (Radimerski et al., 2002; Um et al., 2004; Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Radimerski et al., 2002; Um et al., 2004; Yang et al., 2014.

claim: All three isoforms of AKT are expressed in retina.
source: Consistent with a previous report (Yang et al., 2015), in situ hybridization and Western blot detected all three isoforms of AKT in retina (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization and Western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: Rictor is the essential component of mTORC2.
source: We blocked mTORC2 genetically by deleting its essential component, Rictor (rapamycin-insensitive companion of mTOR) (Guertin et al., 2006; Laplante and Sabatini, 2012).

claim: Rptor is unique to mTORC1, and its deletion totally blocks mTORC1 activity.
